title: Rebalancing
blurb: Bringing a portfolio back to its agreed mix: drift, methods, cheapest tools, and handling pushback.

rows: New employees (all sections), sales team (talk-tracks, role-plays, niche topics); investors as awareness material
About 74 minutes of lessons, plus role-play and the final quiz
Each L.E.A.R.N. stage has: what to know, how to do it, a talk-track, and the investor takeaway

sources: SEBI Master Circular for Mutual Funds (current edition)

lessons.title: Drift in a single year: up and down
What rebalancing does and doesn't do
Measure drift in percentage points, and ask the client
Three methods: calendar, band, calendar + band
The cheapest order of tools, with the worked example
Before selling anything: loads, tax, hybrids, records
The one line, and selling winners without fear
Role-play lab (2): hidden holdings, goal near, recent units
Compliance: dos, don'ts and the final check

a: Rebalancing is a promise kept to the client’s own risk choice.
Moving money between asset classes to bring the portfolio back to its target mix.
Assets grow at different speeds, so the mix changes even if the client does nothing.
₹20 L at 60/40, never rebalanced (equity 12%, debt 7%): equity becomes ≈70% of ≈₹53 L.
Equity +30%, debt +7%: 60/40 becomes ≈65/35; full rebalance moves ≈₹1.1 L to debt.
Equity −25%, debt +7%: 60/40 becomes ≈51/49; rebalance moves ≈₹1.5 L to equity.
Risk control, not higher returns; in a strongly rising market it can end with less.
Current share minus target share, in percentage points: 66% vs 60% = +6 points.
Written target, whole portfolio, drift size, costs, client situation.
Check and rebalance on a fixed date, e.g. yearly.
Act only when drift exceeds a limit, e.g. ±5 points.
Calendar + band: check yearly, act only beyond the band; check early after a sharp move.
New money → redirect income → switch/STP in stages → sell and reinvest.
Check exit loads (per instalment), possible tax (refer to a CA), and record approval.
Multi-asset and balanced advantage funds rebalance inside; the client doesn’t redeem.
Rebalancing restores the same target after drift; a new target follows goal, life or risk changes.
The agreed share of each asset class.
Example: 60% equity, 40% debt.
Remember: Written, for each goal.
Gap between current and target share.
Example: 66% vs 60% target = +6 points.
Remember: Measure on the whole portfolio.
Rebalance on a fixed date.
Example: Every April.
Remember: Simple; may act on tiny drifts.
Rebalance when drift passes a limit.
Example: Act beyond ±5 points.
Remember: Acts only when it matters.
Check yearly; act only beyond the band.
Example: April check, 64.6% → no action.
Remember: Suggested default.
New money to the underweight asset.
Example: ₹15,000 a month to debt for a year.
Remember: No load, no tax.
Move between schemes of the same fund house.
Example: Debt fund → equity fund.
Remember: It is a redemption: check costs.
Transfer a fixed amount in stages.
Example: ₹1.5 L moved over 6 months.
Remember: Smooths a big move.
Charge on redemption within a set period.
Example: Recent SIP units redeemed.
Remember: Check per instalment.
Tax on gains when units are redeemed.
Example: Selling equity units with gains.
Remember: Refer to a CA.
Planned change of target as a goal nears.
Example: 60/40 → 30/70 three years before goal.
Remember: A new target, not a rebalance.
Record of date, drift, action, reason.
Example: Apr 2026: +6.2, moved ₹1.2 L.
Remember: Protects client and firm.
Reluctance to sell what is rising.
Example: “Why sell what’s doing so well?”
Remember: Trim back to the agreed mix.
Reluctance to buy what has fallen.
Example: “Why buy what’s falling?”
Remember: The rule was agreed when calm.
Leaving the portfolio untouched.
Example: “Let’s leave it.”
Remember: 60% became 70% in 10 years.
Pain when rebalancing looks wrong later.
Example: “Equity kept rising after we sold.”
Remember: It controls risk; it isn’t a forecast.

questions.q: What is rebalancing?
o: Restoring the target mix by moving money between asset classes
questions.why: Restoring the target mix by moving money between asset classes. It brings the portfolio back to the agreed mix.

questions.q: Why do portfolios drift?
questions.why: Assets grow at different speeds. The mix changes on its own.

questions.q: In the 10-year example, a 60% equity target drifted to about…
questions.why: 70%. About 70% if never rebalanced.

questions.q: The main job of rebalancing is…
questions.why: Risk control. It keeps risk at the agreed level.

questions.q: A 60% target is now 66%. The drift is…
questions.why: +6 points. Current share minus target share.

questions.q: Which is our suggested default method?
questions.why: Calendar + band. Check yearly; act only beyond the band.

questions.q: With a ±5-point band, a 60% target at 64.6% means…
questions.why: Within band: no action needed. Optional nudge with new money.

questions.q: The cheapest rebalancing tool is…
o: Directing new money to the underweight asset
questions.why: Directing new money to the underweight asset. No exit load, no tax.

questions.q: After equity falls 25% (60/40 start), rebalancing means…
o: Moving money from debt to equity
questions.why: Moving money from debt to equity. About ₹1.5 L from debt to equity in the example.

questions.q: Each switch between funds is…
o: A redemption that may carry load and tax
questions.why: A redemption that may carry load and tax. Check costs; refer tax to a CA.

questions.q: A goal is now 2 years away. The client asks to “rebalance to 60/40”. You…
o: Explain a new target (glide path) is needed
questions.why: Explain a new target (glide path) is needed. That is a target change, not a rebalance.

questions.q: Which is a valid reason to change the target?
questions.why: A life event. Goal, life or risk-profile changes.

questions.q: Why agree the rule in writing at the start?
o: It is required by tax law
Later decisions follow the client’s calm choice
questions.why: Later decisions follow the client’s calm choice. It removes emotion later.

questions.q: Clients in multi-asset or balanced advantage funds…
questions.why: Get rebalancing inside the fund. The fund does the moving.

questions.q: Which statement is compliant?
o: “Rebalancing keeps your risk at the level you chose; it doesn’t guarantee returns.”
questions.why: “Rebalancing keeps your risk at the level you chose; it doesn’t guarantee returns.”. Explain the purpose honestly.

questions.q: A portfolio's mix stays the same if the client does nothing. Why is that wrong?
o: Assets grow at different speeds, so it drifts
questions.why: Assets grow at different speeds, so it drifts.

questions.q: After equity falls, rebalancing can mean:
questions.why: Restoring the target buys the underweight asset.

questions.q: Does rebalancing always produce higher returns?
o: No — its job is risk control; in strong rallies it can end with less
questions.why: Its job is risk control; in strong rallies it can end with less.

questions.q: Can new SIP money be used to rebalance without selling?
o: Yes — cash-flow rebalancing avoids loads and tax
questions.why: Cash-flow rebalancing avoids loads and tax.

questions.q: Is a market view a good reason to change the target mix?
o: Yes, if the view is strong
No — only goal, life or risk-profile changes justify it
questions.why: Only goal, life or risk-profile changes justify it.

questions.q: After a strong year, Rohan's 60/40 portfolio is at 68/32 and he doesn't want to sell equity. What do you do?
o: Explain the band was breached; use new money first, then a partial switch or STP; check loads and tax; record his decision
questions.why: Explain the band was breached; use new money first, then a partial switch or STP; check loads and tax; record his decision.

questions.q: Leela's 60/40 is at 50/50 after a sharp fall and she wants to wait. What do you say?
o: Remind her of the agreed rule; explain buying lower without predicting the bottom; consider staging the move; no market predictions
questions.why: Remind her of the agreed rule; explain buying lower without predicting the bottom; consider staging the move; no market predictions.

questions.q: A client at 62/38 asks to rebalance immediately. What do you explain?
o: It is within the ±5-point band; costs may outweigh benefits; direct new SIP money if anything
questions.why: Explain it is within the ±5-point band; costs may outweigh benefits; use new SIP money if anything.

questions.q: Arun's funds look 80% equity, but he has ₹30 L in PPF and FDs. What do you do?
o: Measure drift on the whole portfolio; his total mix may already be near target
questions.why: Measure drift on the whole portfolio; his total mix may already be near target.

questions.q: Priya's goal is 2 years away and she asks to “rebalance to 60/40”. What do you explain?
o: This needs a new target along the glide path, not a rebalance; agree and record the new target
questions.why: Explain this needs a new target along the glide path, not a rebalance; agree and record the new target.
